title: Every Shortest Word Chain
statement:
You get a start word, an end word and a list words. A chain goes from start to end by changing exactly one letter at each step. Every word in the chain after start must appear in words; start itself does not have to.

Return every chain of the smallest possible length, each one as a list of words from start to end. Return the chains in any order. If no chain exists, return [].

examples.why: Three different routes all take 3 steps. "sat" is a neighbour of "sap" but leads nowhere.
"ab" → "xb" → "xd" → "cd" also works, but it takes 3 steps, and only the shortest chains count.
"dog" is not in the list, so no chain can end there.

constraints: end.length and every word have the same length as start
All words are distinct lowercase strings
The total number of shortest chains is at most a few hundred
hints: Think of words as nodes and one-letter changes as edges. The shortest chains are shortest paths in an unweighted graph. Which search finds those?
BFS from start level by level. A word may be reached from several words of the previous level; for the shortest chains you need all of them, not just the first.

During BFS, record for each newly reached word the list of its parents in the previous level. Mark a whole level as visited only after the level is done. Once end is reached, walk the parent lists back from end to build every chain.

explain.intuition:
Words are nodes, and two words are connected when they differ in one letter. Shortest chains are shortest paths in this unweighted graph, so BFS is the tool. To find neighbours fast, do not compare every pair of words; instead change each position to each of the 26 letters and look the result up in a set.

The hard part is returning every shortest path, not one. Plain BFS marks a word visited the first time it is seen and drops other ways of reaching it at the same distance. So handle a whole level at once: collect, for every word in the next level, every word in the current level that reaches it. Remove the new level from the unvisited set only after the level is finished. When end appears, stop expanding, then build the chains by walking parent links backwards from end. Because only shortest-distance parents are stored, every walk is a shortest chain.
steps: Put words in a set. If end is missing, return []. Remove start from the set.

BFS by levels starting from [start]. For each word in the level, try every one-letter change; if the result is still in the unvisited set, add the current word to its parents list and add it to the next level.
After the level, delete all next-level words from the unvisited set. Stop when end has parents or the level is empty.
Backtrack from end: follow every parent recursively until start, then reverse each collected path.
pitfalls: Marking a word visited as soon as it is first seen inside a level. A second parent in the same level is then lost, and so are the chains through it.
Storing complete paths in the BFS queue for big inputs. Many partial paths share prefixes, and copying them costs much more than parent lists.
Continuing BFS after the level that reaches end. Longer chains would get mixed in.

complexity.time: O(N · L · 26) for the BFS plus the size of the output

solutions.title: BFS over whole paths
solutions.idea: The queue holds full paths. Words used in a level are removed only after that level, so every shortest path survives. Simple, but copies many path prefixes.

solutions.title: Level BFS with parent lists, then backtrack
solutions.idea: BFS stores, for each word, all its parents one level closer to start. Walking those links back from end yields exactly the shortest chains.

followups: Run the BFS from both ends at once. How do you merge the two halves without losing chains?
Only the number of shortest chains is needed. Can you count them without listing them?
